The Southern cavefish Typhlichthys subterraneus attains a maximum recorded standard length of 7.1 centimeters [Li = 7.1 centimeters], a modest size typical of stygobitic amblyopsids inhabiting nutrient-poor groundwater systems. Females produce demersal, yolk-laden eggs with an average diameter of 2.15 millimeters, and the resulting hatchlings emerge at a wet weight of just 0.0052 grams [Wwb = 0.0052 grams], reflecting the limited endogenous reserves available in these oligotrophic habitats. All life-history estimates presented here were derived from individuals maintained under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable water temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C], which approximates the thermal regime of the species' subterranean spring habitats across its range in the karst regions of the central United States. Under these conditions, the yolk-sac larva completes its lecithotrophic phase and the age at hatching or birth is approximately 76 days [ab = approximately 76 days], a protracted embryonic period relative to epigean cypriniform fishes at a temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. This slow developmental pace likely reflects the low metabolic demands and reduced predation pressure characteristic of the cave environment.

The standard length at which individuals achieve sexual maturity or puberty is approximately 3.65 centimeters [Lp = approximately 3.65 centimeters], a threshold determined through histological examination of gonadal recrudescence in preserved museum specimens supplemented by laboratory observations. At this body size, the corresponding wet weight at puberty is about 0.51 grams [Wwp = about 0.51 grams], calculated from the length-weight relationship derived for the species. The time since birth at which this maturational milestone is reached averages 488 days from hatching [tp = 488 days from hatching] when animals are reared at the standard reference temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C], with some inter-individual variation attributable to local food availability and individual growth trajectories. This extended prepubertal period, spanning approximately sixteen months, is consistent with the slow life-history syndrome frequently observed among cave-dwelling teleosts. Comparative data from other Amblyopsidae suggest that delayed maturation is an evolved response to the chronically low resource availability in subterranean aquifers.

An impressive maximum lifespan has been documented for Typhlichthys subterraneus, with the oldest confirmed individual living for 4 years [am = 4 years] in the laboratory environment at 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. This longevity is notable for a fish of its diminutive size and likely reflects a combination of reduced predation, low metabolic turnover, and conservative metabolic expenditure in a stable thermal environment. In contrast to many epigean species that exhibit rapid senescence following first reproduction, the cavefish displays a gradual physiological decline, with some individuals remaining reproductively viable deep into their third and fourth years. The ultimate wet weight attained by adult specimens is approximately 3.7 grams [Wwi = approximately 3.7 grams], achieved as individuals approach their asymptotic size after several years of slow, steady growth. Field surveys in Kentucky and Alabama have occasionally recovered individuals nearing this maximum mass, though most breeding adults weigh between two and three grams.

Reproductive effort in this species is modest, reflecting the energetic constraints of the cave habitat. Gravid females produce a single clutch of eggs annually [F_R_i = single clutch of eggs annually], with each clutch containing 50 eggs [N_R_i = each clutch containing 50 eggs]. This low fecundity, combined with the extended incubation period, results in a relatively low annual reproductive output of roughly 50 eggs per year [Ri = roughly 50 eggs per year] when compared to surface-dwelling congeners. The timing of gametogenesis is closely tied to the stable thermal regime; vitellogenesis onset is triggered by endogenous cues rather than seasonal temperature fluctuations. Given the stable temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C] characteristic of their hypogean environment, individuals adopt a conservative reproductive strategy, investing resources toward somatic maintenance over many years rather than producing large clutches. This iteroparous life history is an adaptation to unpredictable food supply in the cave ecosystem.

The growth trajectory of juvenile Typhlichthys subterraneus is characterized by a slow but steady increase in both length and mass, with the transition from yolk-dependent larva to actively feeding juvenile occurring several weeks after hatching. Sexual maturity, rather than first reproduction, is attained at roughly 488 days from hatching [tp = roughly 488 days from hatching] under the prevailing cave temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C], representing a delayed onset of reproductive potential in this energy-limited troglobite. Understanding the population dynamics of this stygobitic fish is critical for conservation efforts, as its restricted karst distribution makes it vulnerable to groundwater pollution and habitat alteration. This species exemplifies the suite of life-history adaptations common to organisms inhabiting stable, resource-poor subterranean environments.
